title: Part 3: Discovery & Resolution
content_html:
Part 3: Discovery and Resolution

The final part of Coram Boy brings the novel’s two worlds crashing together. Secrets that have been hidden for years are uncovered, and characters must confront the truth about who Aaron really is. Gavin builds towards a climax that is both thrilling and emotionally devastating, weaving together the threads of parentage, revelation, sacrifice and justice.

Aaron’s Parentage Revealed

The central revelation of Part 3 is that Aaron — the foundling boy with the extraordinary singing voice — is the son of Alexander Ashbrook and Melissa. For years, Alexander has believed his child died. Melissa has carried the grief of losing her baby in silence. The discovery that their son is alive, and has been living at the Foundling Hospital under a different name, is the novel’s emotional core.

Key Fact

The revelation of Aaron’s parentage resolves the dramatic irony that has run throughout the novel. The reader has known since Part 1 that Meshak saved the baby, but Alexander, Melissa and Aaron himself have been kept in the dark. When the truth finally emerges, it is both a release of tension and a moment of profound emotional impact.

Gavin handles the reunion with restraint. It is not a simple happy ending — years have been lost, identities have been fractured, and the damage done by Otis’s crimes cannot be fully undone. Alexander must reconcile the privileged world he inhabits with the foundling world his son has grown up in. Aaron must absorb the fact that his entire identity — his name, his history, his place in society — has been a fiction.

Meshak’s Sacrifice

Meshak’s story reaches its climax in Part 3 when he makes the ultimate sacrifice to protect Aaron from Otis. Having defied his father once by saving the baby, Meshak now faces the consequences of that defiance. Otis, realising that Aaron’s survival could expose his crimes, becomes a direct threat to the boy. Meshak places himself between Otis and Aaron, choosing to protect the child he saved even at the cost of his own life.

Meshak’s death is the novel’s most powerful moment. The character whom society would consider the least valuable — a man with a learning disability, the son of a criminal, someone with no status or wealth — turns out to be the most morally courageous person in the story. Gavin uses Meshak’s sacrifice to make a devastating argument: that society’s way of measuring human worth (by class, intelligence, wealth) is fundamentally wrong. Meshak’s selflessness contrasts sharply with every other character who has failed Aaron — from the mothers who handed babies to Otis, to the society that allowed child trafficking to flourish.

Otis’s Villainy Exposed

The truth about Otis Gardiner’s child-collecting scheme is finally brought to light. His years of deception — posing as a Coram man, taking money from desperate mothers, ordering the burial of babies — is exposed. Gavin does not give Otis a dramatic villain’s downfall with speeches or spectacle. Instead, his exposure is almost bureaucratic, reinforcing the idea that his evil was always mundane and systematic rather than theatrical.

Key Fact

Otis’s downfall mirrors the way his crimes were committed — without drama. Gavin makes a deliberate choice not to give the villain a grand ending, because the point is that real evil is often ordinary. The true drama belongs to Meshak’s sacrifice and Aaron’s reunion with his parents.

Resolution and Justice

The novel’s ending offers a qualified sense of resolution. Aaron is reunited with his birth parents. Otis is exposed and punished. The buried babies are acknowledged. But Gavin does not present this as an uncomplicated happy ending. Meshak is dead. The years Aaron spent without a family cannot be returned. The other babies Otis buried are gone forever. Justice comes, but it comes too late and at too high a cost.

The ending asks the reader to hold two truths at once: that justice is possible, and that it is never complete. Aaron gains a family but has lost his foundling identity. Meshak’s goodness saves a life but costs his own. Otis is punished but the system that enabled him — the class inequality, the lack of protection for vulnerable mothers and children — remains unchanged. Gavin refuses to offer simple comfort, instead leaving the reader to reflect on what real justice would look like in a society built on inequality.

Understanding how Part 3 resolves the novel’s conflicts is essential for the exam. Questions about character, theme or structure will all require you to discuss how the ending reflects Gavin’s wider argument about society, justice and human worth.

The resolution also carries structural significance. The dual timeline that has run throughout the novel finally collapses into a single present moment when Aaron’s parentage is revealed. The worlds of privilege and poverty, which Gavin has kept separate for most of the narrative, are forced to confront each other. This structural convergence mirrors Gavin’s thematic argument: the wealthy cannot remain insulated from the suffering their social system creates. The truth will eventually emerge, even if it takes years.
exam_tip_html: When writing about the novel’s resolution in the exam, avoid simply saying ‘it has a happy ending.’ The ending is deliberately complex. Show the examiner you understand this by discussing what is gained (reunion, justice) and what is lost (Meshak’s life, Aaron’s foundling years, the other buried babies). This kind of balanced, nuanced analysis — acknowledging complexity rather than simplifying — is what earns top AO1 marks. Always connect the ending to Gavin’s broader point about 18th-century society.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • The revelation of Aaron’s parentage resolves the dramatic irony that has run through the novel, merging the two timelines and bringing the Ashbrook world into contact with the foundling world.
  • Meshak’s sacrifice is the novel’s emotional climax — the character society values least proves to be the most morally courageous, challenging how we measure human worth.
  • The ending offers qualified justice: Aaron is reunited with his parents and Otis's crimes are exposed, but Thomas Ledbury is dead, years are lost, Otis/Gaddarn disappears without definitive punishment, and the system that enabled the crimes remains unchanged.

glossary_terms.definition: The revealing of a truth that has been hidden from one or more characters, creating a turning point in the narrative.
When the audience knows something the characters do not, creating tension as the reader waits for the truth to emerge.
Giving up something precious, often one's own life, for the sake of another.
The quality of being willing to do what is right regardless of personal cost.
The act of pretending to be legitimate while committing crimes, as Otis does by posing as a Coram man.
The final part of a narrative where conflicts are resolved and the story reaches a settled conclusion.
